papers.title: Adaptive Policy-Guided Error Mitigation (APGEM): A Unified Learning-Based Framework for Noise Resilience in Quantum Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Error mitigation stands between variational quantum algorithms and useful results on today's noisy hardware, yet in practice a mitigation method is usually chosen once, by hand, and applied unchanged for the life of an experiment. This is a poor fit for quantum machine learning (QML), where the circuit and the noise drift as training proceeds, so the best strategy in one regime is often wrong in another. We present a generalized form of Adaptive Policy-Guided Error Mitigation (APGEM), which treats the choice of mitigation technique as an online decision made from an algorithm's own feedback. A single contextual-bandit controller observes signals any variational algorithm already produces, such as fidelity, entropy, reward or loss, and gradient behavior, and selects among Zero-Noise Extrapolation, Probabilistic Error Cancellation, Measurement Error Mitigation, Dynamical Decoupling, and circuit optimization per step. Because it depends only on this shared feedback interface, the framework applies unchanged across supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement, and hybrid quantum-classical learning. Evaluated on five paradigms across 80 algorithm-and-noise conditions, adaptive selection reaches 95.5% of an oracle that always picks the best technique and significantly outperforms all six fixed strategies (Friedman $χ^{2}=92.18$, $p\approx1.1\times10^{-17}$; pairwise Wilcoxon $p<4\times10^{-6}$). The learned policy is noise-aware: its favored technique shifts as depolarizing and readout error rise. On noise models from eight real IBM devices, APGEM tracks the oracle almost exactly (99.9% of oracle utility) at a flat cost of roughly $1.3\times10^{4}$ shots from three to eight qubits.

papers.title: Machine-learning decoders for fusion-based quantum computing in real time
papers.abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires decoders that combine accuracy, throughput, low latency, and scalability to large numbers of physical qubits. In photonic fusion-based architectures, erasures from photon loss and probabilistic fusion measurements are a dominant error mechanism, motivating decoders that remain accurate at high erasure rates. We introduce PRISM, a transformer-based machine-learning decoder designed to exploit the known locations of erasures in protocols subject to both Pauli and erasure errors. We benchmark PRISM across a wide range of fault-tolerant protocols based on surface codes, color codes, and quantum low-density parity-check codes, with distances up to 24. Across these benchmarks, PRISM matches the logical error rates of integer-programming-based decoders while being significantly faster, including at error rates up to 50% of threshold. We further optimize the decoder and its real-time hardware implementation to reduce latency while maintaining accuracy. Our optimized implementation on an AMD VP1902 FPGA can decode logical blocks of distance 8 in both space and time, demonstrating a latency of 6.59 microseconds and an amortized decoding time of 1.56 microseconds per logical block is possible. These results show that machine-learning decoding can provide accurate, low-latency inference for erasure-dominated fault-tolerant quantum architectures.

papers.title: Alchemically Transferable Parameters for Variational Quantum Eigensolvers
papers.abstract: Machine-learned circuit parameters could remove one of the main bottlenecks of variational quantum eigensolvers: the classical optimization loop, with its typical barren plateaus, local minima, and costly energy and gradient evaluations, is replaced by a direct prediction. Prior work showed that machine-learning models paired with a structured circuit design can transfer across system size and structure within hydrogenic systems. The next step: Extending them to organic molecules would seem to require re-training on use-case-specific training sets. In this work, we show that this is not necessary by establishing an alchemical approach. A geometric projection places surrogate hydrogen atoms along the bond directions of the target molecule and so maps its local bonding environment onto small hydrogenic fragments. Existing hydrogenic solvers can then be reused as they are. The only new quantity is a single projection radius per bond type, which is fitted once on a small reference molecule and reused unchanged thereafter. We demonstrate the approach on the separable-pair circuit designs that have been used in prior work and extend the approach to multi-circuit approaches that span effective bases for quantum subspaces.

papers.title: Matched but Not Better: An Equivalence-Tested Benchmark of Quantum Machine Learning on Six Clinical Datasets and the QML-Health-READY Reporting Framework
papers.abstract: Background: Quantum machine learning (QML) is promoted for clinical prediction, but comparisons with classical models are rarely paired or tested for equivalence. Methods: We compared a quantum-kernel support vector machine (QSVM; 4 qubits, tuned bandwidth) and a variational quantum classifier (VQC) with five tuned classical models across six public clinical datasets. All models used identical four-component inputs and 25 cross-validation splits. Paired AUROC differences were assessed using a corrected resampled t-test, Holm-adjusted equivalence tests (margins: +/-0.02 and +/-0.05), and random-effects pooling. Ablation, noise, finite-shot, and implementation-fault analyses were conducted. We propose QML-Health-READY, an eight-domain reporting framework. Results: Neither quantum model significantly outperformed any classical comparator. Pooled across datasets, QSVM differed from the kernel-matched radial basis function (RBF) SVM by -0.006 AUROC (95% CI: -0.017 to +0.004), equivalent to +/-0.02. VQC differed from the best classical model by -0.007 (95% CI: -0.019 to +0.004). QSVM was equivalent to RBF SVM within +/-0.05 in four of six datasets but was significantly worse than the best classical model on NHANES 2017-18 (-0.076). A classically trivial product-state kernel performed as well as the entangling kernel. With depolarizing noise (p = 0.01) and 1,024 shots per kernel entry, QSVM AUROC decreased by 0.054 (95% CI: 0.036 to 0.071). Untuned bandwidth produced near-chance AUROC (0.48-0.59). Conclusions: Correctly configured quantum classifiers approached but did not exceed tuned classical models. Finite-shot estimation, rather than gate noise, was their main practical cost, while configuration errors could reverse conclusions. QML-Health-READY defines reporting requirements for credible claims.

papers.title: Toward On-Chip Training of Spiking Neural Networks for Dense Event-Based Vision
papers.abstract: Event cameras provide low-latency, asynchronous visual sensing for resource-constrained robotics. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) process event streams naturally, but training deep SNNs with backpropagation through time (BPTT) requires substantial memory and remains difficult on neuromorphic hardware. Local learning avoids this by restricting error propagation to local blocks, but existing methods mainly target classification rather than dense prediction. We introduce DELL (Dense Event-driven Local Learning), a block wise scheme for dense event-based vision that replaces global gradient propagation with local dense supervision. Learnable, spatially structured local heads supervise each block at its appropriate resolution while preserving temporal dynamics within blocks. We evaluate DELL on optical-flow regression and semantic segmentation with a fully spiking U-shaped architecture. On DSEC optical flow, DELL reduces peak training memory by 39.6% relative to end-to-end BPTT while improving accuracy, reaching 1.670 px endpoint error on the official test benchmark versus 1.941 px for the same backbone trained end-to-end. Block detachment behaves more like a regularizer than a constraint. DECOLLE, the existing local-learning baseline, relies on fixed random local read-outs poorly suited to dense regression, resulting in a 3.9x higher endpoint error; learnable local heads recover this loss and outperform end-to-end training across all optical-flow metrics. On segmentation, they recover most of the performance gap, although DELL remains a few mIoU points behind end-to-end training. With 2.3M parameters, 24x fewer than the strongest SNN baseline, the backbone remains competitive with the SNN state of the art on DSEC. These results extend local learning to dense event-based prediction while substantially reducing training memory.

papers.title: LiFR v2: Completion-Augmented Event Propagation for High-Rate Dense Prediction
papers.abstract: High-rate dense perception in dynamic environments is limited by the low update rate of RGB cameras, as rapid scene changes can occur between frames. Event cameras offer temporally dense but spatially sparse measurements, complementary to spatially dense RGB observations. Direct fusion cannot fully exploit this complementarity, while event-guided propagation fails on newly appearing or disoccluded regions without valid RGB support. We present LiFR v2, a unified propagation-completion-memory framework for causal anytime and streaming dense prediction from an RGB keyframe and events. LiFR v2 introduces an Event-Guided Completion Module (EGCM) to recover task-relevant representations where propagation is unsupported, and a History Retrieval Module (HRM) to reuse completed representations across successive queries. The framework supports semantic segmentation, monocular depth estimation, and multi-task dense prediction, and we further introduce SHF-Emerge to evaluate rapid object emergence and disocclusion. LiFR v2 achieves 74.37% mIoU on DSEC and 56.13% on SHF-Emerge, improving LiFR-Seg by 1.85 percentage points on the latter, while reducing SHF-Emerge depth RMSE from 1.564 m to 1.118 m over the propagation baseline. It also exceeds 100 FPS for both segmentation and depth, demonstrating accurate and efficient high-rate perception beyond RGB frame rates.

papers.title: Event-Frame Fusion for Inter-Frame Segmentation via Event-Guided Motion
papers.abstract: Autonomous navigation requires precise and efficient semantic segmentation, yet existing frame-based approaches remain limited by motion blur, glare, latency, and the low temporal resolution (20-30 FPS) of conventional cameras, which leads to information loss between frames. Event cameras have emerged as an alternative sensing modality, capturing intensity changes asynchronously with high temporal resolution, high dynamic range, and sparse outputs. However, event-based algorithms still fall short of frame-based ones in accuracy, as most segmentation methods are designed for dense frame data. To overcome these limitations, we propose a hybrid vision architecture that combines conventional frame-based and event-based cameras. The system integrates two complementary components: (1) a compact Spiking Neural Network (SNN) with 42k parameters for motion estimation, and (2) a lightweight event-driven SNN with 0.84M parameters for frame-based semantic segmentation, which interpolates motion between frames to refine segmentation results. By predicting inter-frame segmentations, the framework achieves segmentation rates of up to 500 Hz with an energy consumption below 1.87 mJ per inference, while maintaining real-time GPU execution at frequencies up to 200 Hz. Additionally, our approach compensates for information loss in frames affected by blur or overexposure, enabling more robust perception in challenging conditions.

papers.title: OctoSense: Self-Supervised Learning for Multimodal Robot Perception
papers.abstract: We present OctoSense, an open-source sensor platform with stereo RGB and event cameras, LiDAR, a thermal camera, an inertial measurement unit, RTK-corrected global positioning system, and proprioception (CAN bus data from a car, and joint angles for a quadruped robot). The eponymous OctoSense dataset contains 59 hours of time-synchronized driving data across different types of environments at different times of the day, including situations with highly degraded sensors. We demonstrate multi-modal self-supervised learning using such real-world robotics data, where sensors have different representations, frequencies, latencies and noise. Our approach, a "late-fusion" masked autoencoder, (i) uses modality-specific tokenizers to account for different spatiotemporal characteristics of these sensors, and (ii) caches modality-specific tokens at inference time to process new measurements as they come. This architecture (i) is fast (6.68 ms and 112 ms on NVIDIA 5090 and Orin NX respectively, to compute the representation), (ii) performs better than existing image-only foundation models on tasks such as estimation of optical flow, depth, semantic segmentation, and ego-motion (translation, rotation, and steering angle), and (iii) predicts robustly at nighttime or in situations where sensory data is degraded. See our project page for links to the dataset, code, and supplementary videos: https://abisulco.com/octosense/.

papers.title: Medical Image Segmentation: Foundation Model Adaptation versus Task-Specific Training
papers.abstract: Foundation models pretrained on large natural-image collections are increasingly adapted for medical image segmentation, in the expectation that they will replace models trained for each task. Most comparisons, however, use data from the training distribution and a single task-specific baseline whose configuration is rarely justified, and therefore provide limited evidence of performance at new clinical sites. It also remains unclear how much of a foundation model must be adapted, and what determines this. We adapted a foundation model, DINOv2, with strategies ranging from tuning only its bias terms to full fine-tuning, and compared it with U-Nets and ResU-Nets trained from scratch. Experiments covered colonoscopy, breast ultrasound and dermoscopy, with testing on held-out data from the training source and on independent datasets from other institutions. The adapted foundation model generalised better on every external dataset. Within the training distribution, the task-specific models remained competitive when training data were abundant, and delineated boundaries more precisely, while the foundation model more often missed small lesions. Only a small fraction of the foundation model required adaptation, and the capacity needed was determined by the imaging domain rather than by the adaptation method. A widely used polyp test set was also found to duplicate images from another benchmark. Foundation-model adaptation is therefore warranted where models must work across sites, with capacity selected on the target domain.

papers.title: Differentiable Inverse Rendering Recovers Intrinsic Properties from Intravascular Optical Coherence Tomography
papers.abstract: Medical images encode intrinsic tissue properties that indicate disease progression, yet these properties remain entangled with the system-dependent physics of image formation. Differentiable inverse rendering asks whether they are recoverable by inverting the imaging system's forward physics rather than through post-hoc correction. We address this in optical coherence tomography (OCT), focusing on the optical attenuation coefficient, a per-pixel marker of pathology and cellular composition. Conventional recovery relies on closed-form inversions limited to simplified light-tissue models, or learned methods coupled to specific imaging configurations. We instead recover per-pixel attenuation from a single OCT image by gradient descent through a differentiable physics-based forward model. We verified the method against analytical solutions, validated it on five in vitro phantoms, and applied it without modification to 29{,}269 clinical intravascular OCT images from 128 patients. The inversion needs no training data or segmentations and is portable across platforms and retrospective archives. Replacing the forward model or recovering another optical parameter leaves the optimization procedure unchanged. We demonstrate per-pixel recovery is tractable because gradient information scales to this high-dimensional problem, where gradient-free methods become intractable. Our work supports quantitative tissue characterization from OCT images and provides a framework for extension across imaging modalities and organ systems.

papers.title: 3D Segmentation in the Clinic: A Grand Challenge
papers.abstract: This paper describes the set-up of a segmentation competition for automatic and semi-automatic extraction of the liver from computed tomography scans and the caudate nucleus from brain MRI data. This competition was held in the form of a workshop at the 2007 Medical Image Computing and Computer Assisted Intervention conference. The rationale for organizing the competition is discussed, the training and test data sets for both segmentation tasks are described and the scoring system used to evaluate the segmentation is presented.

papers.title: Frequency-consistent synthesis and selective transfer for medical image analysis
papers.abstract: Complementary imaging is not always available, and realistic synthesis does not necessarily improve downstream analysis. Here we introduce a training framework linking medical image synthesis to task learning through adaptive frequency consistency and selective feature transfer. Image-specific frequency constraints encourage consistency of structure and detail. Features are transferred only when a teacher using synthetic images achieves a lower task-error score than the student by a task-specific margin on a labelled training sample. Evaluations across five datasets show improved translation fidelity with three adversarial and diffusion-based translators trained without paired supervision, alongside gains in brain-tumour segmentation on tumour-containing slices and lesion centre-point detection. All 105 reported paired comparisons yielded point estimates favouring the proposed methods, including 36 external translation comparisons on post?treatment MRI without retraining. These findings support synthetic modalities as task-oriented complements to acquired scans when complementary imaging is unavailable.

papers.title: Where, How, and When: Query-Guided Grounding for Video Understanding
papers.abstract: Understanding video content requires reasoning at multiple levels of granularity, from identifying objects to interpreting their interactions and localizing when specific actions occur. This thesis studies three query-guided grounding tasks that answer where key objects are (object-level grounding), how they interact (relationship-level grounding), and when specific moments occur (moment-level grounding). For object-level grounding, we present QDETRv, a query-guided extension of the Detection Transformer for one-shot localization of unseen objects in videos, which combines query-context fusion, a memory module for temporal consistency, and unsupervised pretraining on synthetic object trajectories. We further propose the Temporal Object-Aware Vision Transformer (TOViT) for few-shot video object detection, which builds on a language-aligned open-set vision encoder and propagates high-confidence object features across frames. For relationship-level grounding, we introduce few-shot referring relationships in videos: given a (subject, predicate, object) query and a few support videos sharing the predicate, the entities are localized by optimizing a T-partite random field using a meta-learned relation network with query-conditioned translational embeddings, Global Semantic Aggregation, Local Localization Aggregation, and belief-propagation-based message passing. For moment-level grounding, we propose the Moment Alignment Transformer (MATR) for video-to-video moment retrieval, which uses dual-stage Dynamic Time Warping for pre- and post-fusion alignment, learnable queries for boundary prediction, and self-supervised pretraining with temporal augmentations; MATR also extends to text-to-video moment retrieval with performance comparable to, or better than, the state of the art. These contributions advance query-guided video understanding across spatial, relational, and temporal grounding.

papers.title: Your Model Already Knows Don't Teach It, Learn to Ask It: Soft Prompting for Few-Shot Adaptation of Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: We address few-shot object detection with vision-language models (VLMs) in out-of-domain settings such as aerial, industrial, and medical imagery, using only ten annotated images for supervision. Existing adaptation methods are discrete prompt optimization and LoRA fine-tuning. We revisit a third option: soft prompting, where a small number of continuous prompt tokens are optimized while the pretrained backbone remains frozen. We identify two key design choices. First, placing prompt tokens at the cross-modal boundary between visual and text tokens outperforms other placements (10.0 vs. 8.4 mAP). Second, initializing prompts from the empty space token outperforms semantic and random initialization. With these choices, one to three learned tokens (7,168 parameters on average) match the best LoRA configuration on Roboflow20-VL (14.2 mAP, 10-shot) while training over 20,000x fewer parameters. Soft prompting remains harder to optimize, exhibiting higher variance across random seeds. Unlike LoRA, however, it causes no forgetting: the LoRA rank matching our accuracy reduces NaturalBench VQA accuracy by 35% relative, rising to 56% at the largest rank, whereas soft prompting leaves pretrained performance unchanged. The learned tokens behave like prompts rather than weights. They transfer to a newer model without retraining (+0.8 mAP on Qwen3.5-9B) and can be verbalized into readable prompts competitive with prompt-search methods (matching DetPO and outperforming GEPA). The approach also extends beyond detection. On RoboCasa manipulation tasks, the frozen $π_{0.5}$ vision-language-action policy benefits from soft prompting, matching the LoRA baseline on two of three tasks when tokens are placed at the gradient bottleneck. These results suggest modern VLMs already encode much of what is needed for specialized domains; the challenge is learning how to ask.

papers.title: SAM3-O2D2: Zero-Shot Object Out-of-Distribution Detection by Object Class Prompting of the SAM3-Image Model
papers.abstract: Object detectors have shown remarkable performance in various fields, among these medical imaging, surveillance, and autonomous driving. However, they are prone to overconfidence when encountering unseen objects in real-world deployments, causing potential safety issues. To address this, detecting out-of-distribution (OOD) objects is essential for reliable object detection. Modern approaches leverage the broad semantic knowledge of foundation models such as CLIP for post-hoc few- and zero-shot OOD detection. However, these methods typically perform OOD assessment in feature space, which can be sensitive to object detector localization errors and variations in object appearance. Moreover, the current state-of-the-art (SOTA) zero-shot method performs computationally costly diffusion in inference. In this work, for our proposed zero-shot object OOD detection method SAM3-O2D2, we employ the SAM3-image foundation model in an efficient manner. Specifically, we prompt SAM3 only with the object detector's predicted classes and compare the predictions of the object detector and SAM3. An object is in-distribution (ID), if SAM3 also detects an object at the corresponding location. If SAM3 does not detect the prompted object, this indicates a mismatch between the detector's prediction and the image content, suggesting that the object is OOD. Experimental results show that our method significantly surpasses the so-far zero-shot SOTA method. Specifically, we achieve new SOTA AuROC and FPR95 metrics over both ID datasets Pascal-VOC and BDD100K and both OOD datasets MS-COCO and OpenImages.

papers.title: ProtoRAG: Prototype-Based Retrieval Augmentation for Few-Shot Fine-Grained Remote Sensing Object Detection
papers.abstract: Few-shot fine-grained object detection (FGOD) in remote sensing imagery is challenging because limited annotations must support both object localization and discrimination among visually similar subcategories. Although multimodal large language models (MLLMs) provide strong coarse object localization, they lack explicit visual evidence for reliable fine-grained recognition. To address this limitation, we propose ProtoRAG, a prototype-based retrieval-augmented framework that decouples coarse localization from fine-grained recognition by equipping MLLMs with an external object-level visual memory. To construct a reliable visual memory from limited support samples, we introduce Discriminative Prototype Space Learning (DPSL), which encourages discriminative and prototype-stable representations through supervised contrastive learning and prototype-consistency regularization. We further develop an uncertainty-guided candidate-constrained reasoning strategy that augments MLLMs with retrieved candidate-specific visual references and invokes multimodal reasoning only for ambiguous instances. Extensive experiments show that ProtoRAG consistently surpasses representative baselines in nine few-shot settings, outperforming the strongest baselines by 14.80, 2.27, and 4.04 mAP$_{50}$ on MAR20, HRSC2016, and FAIR1M-2.0, respectively.

papers.title: Distribution Shift Detection in Remote Sensing Imagery using Machine Learning Models
papers.abstract: Remote sensing imagery acquired by Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) supports wide range of applications; however, deploying machine learning (ML) models on resource-constrained aerial platforms introduces challenges beyond predictive accuracy, particularly when deployment data differ from the distributions observed during training. Such shifts are common in remote sensing due to geographic, sensor, seasonal, and other visual variations. A practical solution is to equip deployed models with mechanisms that detect emerging distribution shifts and support subsequent responsive actions. This paper presents an empirical case study of three open-source detection tools: (i) Alibi-Detect; (ii) NannyML; and (iii) PyTorch-OOD. Using cross-dataset remote-sensing shifts, we evaluate both detection effectiveness and computational latency of these tools. Our results reveal differences in detection behavior and processing cost across methods and implementations, highlighting trade-offs between detection capability and response-time. These findings motivate further work toward lightweight, and latency-aware monitoring mechanisms for resource-constrained systems.

papers.title: ChangeJEPA: Predict Before You Compare for Remote Sensing Change Detection
papers.abstract: Remote sensing change detection is typically formulated as Siamese feature comparison, where two images are encoded independently and a decoder determines which discrepancies correspond to meaningful change. This is challenging because the encoders preserve both true scene changes and nuisance variations such as illumination, seasonal, radiometric, and geometric differences. We introduce ChangeJEPA, a bitemporal joint-embedding predictive architecture that reformulates change detection as latent post-state prediction. Given a pre-change image and partial post-change evidence, ChangeJEPA predicts the full post-change representation under two complementary conditions: a prior hypothesis derived from the pre-change scene and an updated hypothesis conditioned on observed post-change context. A joint-embedding predictive loss aligns both hypotheses with the target latent representation, encouraging semantic consistency while suppressing transient appearance variations. Change is then inferred from the disagreement among the pre-change representation, the observed post-change target, and the predicted latent states, capturing complementary evidence of change, prior surprise, contextual update, and prediction reliability. Across SYSU-CD, LEVIR-CD+, and CDD, ChangeJEPA consistently outperforms its decoder matched Siamese baseline by up to 1.51 IoU points and achieves the best IoU and F1-score on all three benchmarks, demonstrating the advantage of latent post-state prediction over direct feature comparison. Page: https://buddhi19.github.io/ChangeJEPA

papers.title: ArabGeoText: Tool-Augmented Vision-Language Models for Arabic Geospatial Text Spotting
papers.abstract: Geospatial text spotting involves locating and transcribing geographic labels, such as road names, district names, and landmarks, in raster maps. These labels are often small, densely arranged, and arbitrarily oriented. Although Arabic text recognition has been studied extensively in documents and natural scenes, Arabic geospatial text spotting remains underexplored. We introduce ARABGEOTEXT, an Arabic-centric benchmark covering 970 geographic locations in Riyadh and Jeddah, with 17,875 manually annotated text instances per view type. For each location, we pair an OpenStreetMap (OSM) rendering with a composite created by overlaying that rendering on the corresponding remote sensing (RS) imagery. The paired views preserve label content and pixel geometry, allowing evaluation across different backgrounds. Geographic partitions support in-city and city-disjoint evaluation of detection, recognition, and end-to-end spotting. Experiments with direct Qwen3.5-4B spotting show difficulties in recovering all labels within a tile. We therefore propose a tool-augmented vision-language framework that combines YOLO26 localization and crop rectification with Qwen3.5-4B recognition adapted through low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The framework outperforms direct LoRA-adapted Qwen3.5-4B spotting across both image views and test cities. With localization held fixed, reader adaptation further improves recognition over the pretrained zero-shot reader. The dataset and code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/yakoubbazi/ArabGeoText.

papers.title: HyperFlow: Class-Incremental Semantic Change Detection via Hyperbolic Flow
papers.abstract: Semantic change detection in remote sensing aims to identify and characterize land-cover transitions observed in pairs of satellite or aerial images. Existing methods assume a fixed set of change categories, limiting their applicability in real-world scenarios where changes of interest may vary, for example across geographies or over time. In this work, we tackle the problem of class-incremental semantic change detection, where a model progressively learns to detect new types of semantic change. To do so, we exploit the hierarchical structure of land-cover semantics, where newly introduced categories correspond to fine-grained refinements of existing ones, and represent said semantic categories in hyperbolic space, which is particularly well suited to represent such hierarchical relationships. To capture semantic changes, we introduce HyperFlow, a method relying on Busemann prototypes, modeling change as an anomaly in a learned semantic flow within the hyperbolic embedding space induced by segmentation. HyperFlow couples change detection to class-incremental semantic segmentation, enabling class-incremental semantic change detection. We also present HiChange, a new large-scale, high resolution remote sensing dataset with detailed, fine-grained hierarchical labels. Experimental results demonstrate that HyperFlow achieves both strong change detection and semantic segmentation performance across incremental steps. In particular, we show that progressively refining semantic categories, rather than considering them all directly, yields improved change detection, highlighting the benefits of incremental learning for semantic change detection.
